summary: Specifies how message bodies are handled in SIP and defines user agent support for MIME in message bodies.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how SIP user agents handle message bodies, including bodies with multiple MIME parts. It specifies which parts must be understood, when an unsupported part causes an error, and how a part can be linked to a reference.

questions: how does sip handle message bodies
what is multipart mixed in sip
what is the sip handling parameter
what is the by-reference disposition type
subtitle: Rules for SIP message bodies, MIME parts, content handling, and references between parts.

tldr.problem: SIP extensions increasingly used multipart message bodies, but the base specification did not require user agents to support them or fully define how to process them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires parsing multipart bodies, sets rules for the handling parameter and references to body parts, and defines the by-reference disposition type.
tldr.outcome: SIP user agents have clearer rules for accepting and processing message bodies. RFC 5621 updates RFC 3204, RFC 3261, and RFC 3459, and is updated by RFC 8262.

today: RFC 5621 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2009. It updates RFC 3204, RFC 3261, and RFC 3459, and is updated by RFC 8262.

sections.title: Why SIP Needs Body-Handling Rules
sections.content:
A SIP message has a start line, headers, and an optional body. Headers such as Content-Type, Content-Disposition, and Content-Encoding describe the body. A body can contain multiple MIME parts.

RFC 3261 relied on other specifications for some body rules, and later SIP extensions began using multipart content. RFC 5621 adds background and requirements for areas that needed clarification. Implementers still need to follow RFC 3261 and its referenced specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP messages can carry content in addition to their headers. This RFC clarifies how a recipient identifies and processes that content.

sections.title: Encoding Binary Message Bodies
sections.content:
SIP proxies are eight-bit safe and can carry binary bodies. User agents SHOULD use the binary transfer encoding for all SIP payloads, including binary ones, rather than encoding them as base64.

A user agent MAY use another encoding when it transfers application data between applications that can handle only that encoding. SIP can use S/MIME to protect message bodies; a server that cannot decrypt a body or body part can report that with response 493, Undecipherable.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP can carry binary bodies without converting them to base64. A user agent may use another encoding when the receiving application requires it.

sections.title: Multipart Bodies and User-Agent Support
sections.content:
User agents MUST parse multipart bodies, including nested parts, and MUST support multipart/mixed and multipart/alternative. Support for multipart/related is optional. An unknown multipart subtype is treated as multipart/mixed.

Parts in multipart/alternative contain alternative forms of the same information, ordered from less rich to richer; the recipient selects the last form it understands. A multipart/related body is a compound object with a root part identified by its start parameter or, by default, its first part. User agents SHOULD avoid unnecessary nesting.
sections.plainLanguage: A multipart body contains several parts with a defined structure. User agents must parse mixed and alternative bodies, and may support related bodies when needed.

sections.title: Disposition and the handling Parameter
sections.content:
Content-Disposition describes how a body or body part should be handled. Its handling parameter tells a receiving server what to do when it does not understand required content: optional means ignore it, while required means return 415, Unsupported Media Type. The default is required.

For multipart/mixed and multipart/related, the whole body and its top-level parts can have independently chosen handling values. For multipart/alternative, the body and its top-level parts MUST share a disposition type, and the receiver processes the alternatives according to the whole body's handling value.
sections.plainLanguage: The handling value says whether a recipient may ignore content it does not understand. Required content can cause a 415 response when the recipient cannot process it in that context.

sections.title: References to Body Parts
sections.content:
A Content-ID URL in a header or another body part can refer to a particular body part. User agents MUST generate only forward references: the referenced body part must appear after the element that names it. This lets a recipient process parts while reading the message.

A body part with the by-reference disposition must be handled according to a reference earlier in the same SIP message. If a recipient cannot find that reference, it MUST NOT process the part. If handling was required, the user agent must report an error.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can point to a body part and define how to use it. A by-reference part must not be processed unless the recipient finds its earlier reference.

sections.title: Security and Registered Disposition Type
sections.content:
RFC 5621 adds no new security mechanism. It notes that SIP can protect information hop by hop and end to end, and that S/MIME can encrypt and integrity-protect message bodies as described by RFC 3261.

IANA registered the by-reference Content-Disposition type and updated the registry entry for the handling parameter to cite this specification and related RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP can use S/MIME to protect a message body end to end. IANA also registered the new by-reference disposition type.
